content: This review is part of a series examining primary medical treatments for chronic rhinosinusitis, a condition characterized by inflammation of the nasal and paranasal sinus linings. This inflammation leads to symptoms such as nasal blockage, nasal discharge, facial pain or pressure, and loss of smell. Chronic rhinosinusitis can occur with or without nasal polyps. Systemic and topical antibiotics are used to target infection in the short term and, in some cases, to reduce inflammation over the long term. The goal of these treatments is to normalize nasal mucus and alleviate symptoms. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of systemic and topical antibiotics in individuals with chronic rhinosinusitis. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, with the last search performed on September 29, 2015. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a follow-up period of at least three months, comparing systemic or topical antibiotics to placebo, no treatment, or other pharmacological interventions. Five RCTs involving 293 participants were included in the review. All studies compared systemic antibiotics to either placebo or another pharmacological treatment. The studies varied in their design, making direct comparisons challenging. Four studies included only adults, while one focused on children. Three studies used macrolide antibiotics, one used tetracycline, and one used a cephalosporin. Three studies included patients with chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps, one included patients with nasal polyps, and one had a mixed population. Follow-up periods ranged from 10 to 12 weeks after treatment completion. Systemic Antibiotics vs. Placebo Three studies (176 participants) compared systemic antibiotics to placebo. One study (64 participants, without polyps) assessed disease-specific quality of life using the SNOT-20 scale (0 to 5, with 0 indicating the best quality of life). At the end of the three-month treatment, the group receiving macrolide antibiotics showed a modest improvement in quality of life compared to the placebo group (mean difference: -0.54 points, 95% confidence interval: -0.98 to -0.10). This represents a moderate effect size favoring antibiotics, based on moderate-quality evidence. However, three months after treatment, it was unclear if any difference persisted. Another study (33 participants, with polyps) reported on gastrointestinal disturbances and suspected allergic reactions (e.g., rash or skin irritation) following a short course of tetracycline antibiotics compared to placebo. The evidence was very uncertain regarding whether antibiotics increased the risk of gastrointestinal disturbances (risk ratio: 1.36, 95% CI: 0.22 to 8.50) or skin irritation (risk ratio: 6.67, 95% CI: 0.34 to 128.86), as the quality of evidence was very low. Systemic Antibiotics Plus Saline Irrigation and Intranasal Corticosteroids vs. Placebo Plus Saline Irrigation and Intranasal Corticosteroids One study (60 participants, with and without polyps) compared a three-month course of macrolide antibiotics to placebo, with all participants also using saline irrigation and 70% using intranasal corticosteroids. Disease-specific quality of life was measured using the SNOT-22 scale (0 to 110, with 0 indicating the best quality of life). However, the data were highly skewed, and baseline imbalances made interpretation difficult. It was unclear if there was a meaningful difference between groups at any time point (low-quality evidence). Participants also rated their symptom improvement on a five-point scale (-2 for desperately worse to 2 for cured) at the end of treatment. There was no significant difference in symptom improvement between the antibiotics and placebo groups (risk ratio: 1.50, 95% CI: 0.81 to 2.79; very low-quality evidence). Slightly more participants in the antibiotics group reported feeling worse after treatment. Gastrointestinal disturbances were similar between groups (risk ratio: 1.07, 95% CI: 0.16 to 7.10). General quality of life, measured using the SF-36, showed no difference between groups at the end of treatment or two weeks later. Systemic Antibiotics vs. Intranasal Corticosteroids One study (43 participants, without polyps) compared a three-month course of macrolide antibiotics to intranasal corticosteroids. Patient-reported disease severity was assessed using a composite symptom score (0 to 40, with 0 indicating no symptoms). The results were very uncertain, as the severity scores were similar between groups (mean difference: -0.32, 95% CI: -2.11 to 1.47; low-quality evidence). Systemic Antibiotics vs. Oral Corticosteroids One study (28 participants, with polyps) compared a short course of tetracycline antibiotics (approximately 20 days) to a 20-day course of oral corticosteroids. Data on primary efficacy outcomes could not be extracted. It was uncertain if there was a difference in gastrointestinal disturbances (risk ratio: 1.00, 95% CI: 0.16 to 6.14) or skin irritation (risk ratio: 2.00, 95% CI: 0.20 to 19.62), as the results were similar between groups (very low-quality evidence). Authors' Conclusions The review found limited evidence supporting the effectiveness of systemic antibiotics in treating chronic rhinosinusitis. Moderate-quality evidence suggested a modest improvement in disease-specific quality of life in adults with chronic rhinosinusitis without polyps who received a three-month course of macrolide antibiotics. This improvement was moderate (0.5 points on a five-point scale) and observed only at the end of treatment; no difference was seen three months later. Although antibiotics are generally associated with adverse effects, such as gastrointestinal disturbances, the evidence in this review was very uncertain due to the small size of the studies and the low number of reported events. No RCTs of topical antibiotics met the inclusion criteria. Further research is needed, particularly to evaluate long-term outcomes and adverse effects.
